title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design Telegram

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design a cloud-based messaging platform like Telegram supporting 700M MAU, 1:1 chats, group chats (up to 200K members), broadcast channels (unlimited subscribers), bots, voice/video calls, secret chats with end-to-end encryption (E2EE), and the MTProto protocol — focusing on massive fan-out (channel broadcasts to millions), multi-datacenter geo-replication, and secret chat key exchange. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **1:1 cloud chats**: messages stored on Telegram's servers; multi-device sync; history since account creation.
- **Group chats**: up to 200,000 members; per-group message history; admin roles; slow-mode (rate-limit members).
- **Channels**: one-to-many broadcast; unlimited subscribers; only admins can post; view counters.
- **Secret chats**: end-to-end encrypted (E2EE) 1:1 chats; per-device keys; not stored on server in plaintext; self-destruct timers; read receipts.
- **Bots**: third-party bots receive messages via long-polling or webhook; can send messages, inline keyboards, payments.
- **Media**: photos, videos (up to 2 GB), files (up to 2 GB), voice messages, stickers, GIFs; server-side transcoding.
- **Voice/video calls**: 1:1 E2E encrypted WebRTC calls; group voice chats in channels.
- **Message features**: edit (within 48 h), delete (for both sides, unlimited time), forward, reply, reactions, polls, pinned messages.
- **Search**: search messages within chats; global people/channel search.
- **Multi-device**: same account on phone + desktop + web simultaneously; cloud chats sync to all; secret chats are per-device (no multi-device for E2EE by default — Telegram's design choice).
- **Push notifications**: FCM/APNs for offline users; in-house push for Telegram's own push service.
- **Sync across datacenters**: low-latency replication across DCs (Amsterdam, Miami, Singapore) for global users.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.99 % (Telegram is critical communication in some regions).
- **Latency**: message delivery p99 < 200 ms within a DC; < 500 ms cross-DC; channel broadcast p99 < 5 s to all subscribers.
- **Scale**: 700M MAU, 60M concurrent connections, 500M daily active users, ~15B messages/day, peak 500k msg/s; channels can have 1M+ subscribers (e.g., news channels).
- **Durability**: cloud chats stored forever (Telegram's selling point); secret chat messages stored only as encrypted blobs (server can't read).
- **Privacy**: secret chats E2EE with Diffie-Hellman key exchange; cloud chats encrypted at rest (server-side); metadata minimized.
- **Bandwidth**: 500k msg/s × 2 KB avg = 1 GB/s = 8 Gbps; media uploads ~500 TB/day.
- **MTProto**: custom protocol over TCP/HTTP; reduces round-trips with "request-response combining"; obfuscation to evade censorship.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Connections**: 60M concurrent × 32 KB/connection = ~2 TB RAM across proxy/gateway servers. ~2000 servers at 1 GB each (headroom).
- **Throughput**: 15B msg/day ≈ 175k/s avg, 500k/s peak. Channel broadcasts multiply: 1 message to 1M-subscriber channel = 1M fan-out events; a popular channel posting 10×/day = 10M fan-outs/day per channel. Total fan-out: ~50B events/day.
- **Storage**: 15B msg/day × 1 KB (text+metadata) × forever = 5.5 PB/year. Media: 10 % of messages × 1 MB avg × forever = 550 PB/year. Total ~550 PB/year — Telegram actually uses a custom storage cluster.
- **Bandwidth**: 500k msg/s × 2 KB = 1 GB/s = 8 Gbps just for messages; media egress ~50 Gbps peak.
- **Channels**: top 1000 channels avg 500k subscribers; a single post = 500k fan-outs; 10 posts/day = 5M fan-outs/day per channel; top 1000 channels = 5B fan-outs/day = 60k/s avg.
- **Secret chats**: < 5 % of total traffic (most users use cloud chats); key exchange is rare (per chat initiation).

### Scope
In scope: cloud chats, group chats, channels, secret chats (E2EE), bots, media, multi-DC replication, MTProto, push. Out of scope: voice/video call media servers (WebRTC), Telegram's exact proprietary optimizations, client UI.

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **MTProto Proxy / Frontend**: terminates TCP/HTTP connections from clients; speaks MTProto v2 (encrypted, obfuscated); 2000 instances globally. Handles request-response combining. 2. **Connection Layer (Proxy)**: stateful; per-connection queue of pending updates; pushes updates to clients when they're online; clients fetch missed updates via `updates.getDifference`. 3. **API Core (Backend)**: stateless microservices handling `messages.send`, `messages.getHistory`, `channels.read`, etc. Written in Go/C++ for performance. 4. **Session Manager**: per-user session state (auth_key, device_id, last_seq, last_pts); Redis-backed; tracks which updates each client has received. 5. **Message Storage**: custom KV store or Postgres-sharded by `user_id`; messages stored per-user (each recipient has their own copy in cloud chats — simplifies per-user delete and search). 6. **Channel Fanout Service**: specialized for channels; uses "fan-out-on-write" for small channels, "fan-out-on-read" for huge channels (> 10k subscribers). 7. **Media Service**: handles uploads (chunked, resumable); S3-compatible storage; transcoding pipeline (FFmpeg) for video thumbnails and re-encoding. 8. **Bot Service**: HTTP webhooks to bot owners; long-polling fallback; bot API rate limiting. 9. **Secret Chat Service**: handles E2EE key exchange (Diffie-Hellman); stores encrypted message blobs (can't decrypt); per-device delivery. 10. **Push Service**: in-house push (Telegram's own notification service for users who installed Telegram's app); FCM/APNs fallback. 11. **Cross-DC Replication**: async replication of all writes across 3 DCs (Amsterdam, Miami, Singapore); conflict-free (each write has DC-of-origin timestamp). 12. **Storage**: shard-by-user_id KV store for messages (Telegram uses a custom system, but Postgres+Citus or ScyllaDB are valid designs); Redis for session state; S3-compatible for media. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Client[Mobile / Desktop Client
MTProto v2] --> PROXY[MTProto Proxy x2000
stateful connections] PROXY --> API[API Core
messages.send, getHistory...] API --> SM[Session Manager
Redis: auth_key, last_seq, last_pts] API --> MS[Message Storage
KV shard by user_id] API --> CF[Channel Fanout Service
hybrid: write-fanout small, read-fanout large] CF --> MS API --> MEDIA[Media Service
chunked upload + transcode] MEDIA --> S3[(S3-compatible
media storage)] API --> BOT[Bot Service
webhook / long-poll] BOT --> BotOwner[Bot Owner Server] API --> SC[Secret Chat Service
DH key exchange + E2EE] SC --> MS API --> PUSH[Push Service
in-house + FCM/APNs] API --> K[(Kafka: events
cross-DC replication)] K --> REPL[Cross-DC Replicator] REPL --> DC2[(DC Miami)] REPL --> DC3[(DC Singapore)] PROXY <-.updates push.-> Client ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ MTProto v2 (TCP/HTTP, encrypted, obfuscated) +-----------+ | Client | --------------------------------------------------> | Proxy | | phone/web | <--- updates push (async) ----------------------- | x2000 | | /desktop | +-----+-----+ +-----------+ | v +-----------+ stateless RPC +--------+ +--------+ +-------+----+ | Session | <-----------------> | API |-->| Chan. |--->| Message | | Manager | (auth_key, | Core | | Fanout | | Storage | | (Redis) | last_seq,pts) +---+----+ +---+----+ | (KV shard | +-----------+ | | | user_id) | v v +-------+----+ +-----+----+ +----+-----+ | | Media | | Secret | | | Service | | Chat Svc | <----------+ +----+-----+ | (E2EE) | | | v +----------+ v v | +----+-----+ +----+----+ | Push Svc | | S3 | | (FCM/APNs| | (media) | | + in-hse)| +---------+ +----------+ | +------+-------+------+-------+ | | | v v v +------+------+ +----+------+ +-----+------+ | Kafka | | Bot Svc | | Cross-DC | | events | | webhook | | Replicator | +------+------+ +-----------+ +------+------+ | | v v +----+----+ +-----+-----+ |consumers| | DC Miami | +--> DC Singapore +---------+ +-----------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. Client connects to nearest MTProto Proxy (geo-DNS); handshake negotiates auth_key (already established on first login); connection stays open with keepalive. 2. Client calls `messages.sendMessage(peer=user_id, text="hi", random_id=R)` to Proxy → forwards to API Core. 3. API Core: (a) validates auth; (b) creates a message ID; (c) writes the message to sender's Message Storage (outbox) and recipient's Message Storage (inbox) — two copies for cloud chats; (d) increments sender's `seq` and recipient's `pts`; (e) publishes an `update` to Session Manager for both sender and recipient. 4. Session Manager enqueues the update for each device session: sender's devices get `updateMessageSent` (ack); recipient's devices get `updateNewMessage` (new message). 5. Proxy checks the recipient's connected sessions (via Session Manager); if online, pushes the update immediately over MTProto; if offline, enqueues a push notification. 6. Cross-DC: if sender is in Amsterdam DC and recipient's home DC is Miami, the Amsterdam API Core replicates the write to Miami via Kafka cross-DC replicator; Miami DC owns the recipient's Session Manager and pushes. 7. Channel broadcast: `channels.sendMessage(channel=C, text=...)` → Channel Fanout Service decides strategy: small channel (< 10k subs) writes to each subscriber's storage (fan-out-on-write); large channel (> 10k subs) writes once to channel storage and subscribers fetch via `channels.getMessages` on app open (fan-out-on-read with push notification "new post in C"). 8. Secret chat: `messages.sendEncrypted(peer=secret_chat_id, encrypted_blob)` → Secret Chat Service stores the blob (can't decrypt); recipient fetches; client-side decrypts with the shared E2E key (established via DH at chat creation). 9. Media: client requests upload URL → chunked upload to Media Service → service stores in S3 → returns `file_id` → client references in `messages.sendMedia`.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

```sql
-- Cloud chat messages: stored PER-USER (each participant has their own copy)
-- Sharded KV store; presented here as Postgres for clarity.
CREATE TABLE messages (
    user_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- owner of this copy
    peer_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- the other party or channel
    peer_type     SMALLINT NOT NULL,         -- 1=user, 2=chat, 3=channel
    msg_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- per-(user_id, peer_id) monotonic
    global_msg_id BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- snowflake, for cross-DC dedup
    sender_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    text          TEXT,
    media_id      BIGINT,
    reply_to_msg  BIGINT,
    forwarded_from BIGINT,
    edit_date     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    views         INT,                       -- for channel posts
    read_state    BOOLEAN DEFAULT false,
    date          TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, peer_id, msg_id)
) ;

CREATE TABLE dialogs (
    user_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    peer_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    peer_type    SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    top_message  BIGINT NOT NULL,
    unread_count INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    pinned       BOOLEAN DEFAULT false,
    last_read    BIGINT DEFAULT 0,
    date         TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, peer_id)
);

CREATE TABLE chats (   -- group chats
    chat_id      BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    title        TEXT,
    type         SMALLINT,             -- 1=small group, 2=supergroup, 3=channel
    creator_id   BIGINT,
    members_count INT,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE chat_members (
    chat_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    role       SMALLINT NOT NULL,         -- 0=member, 1=admin, 2=owner
    joined_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    invite_date TIMESTAMPTZ,
    banned     BOOLEAN DEFAULT false,
    PRIMARY KEY (chat_id, user_id)
);

CREATE TABLE channels (   -- broadcast channels; messages stored centrally
    channel_id  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    username    TEXT UNIQUE,
    title       TEXT,
    creator_id  BIGINT,
    subscribers_count BIGINT,
    last_msg_id BIGINT DEFAULT 0,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE channel_messages (
    channel_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    msg_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- per-channel monotonic
    sender_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- admin
    text       TEXT,
    media_id   BIGINT,
    views      INT DEFAULT 0,
    date       TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, msg_id)
);

CREATE TABLE channel_subscriptions (
    channel_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    last_read_msg BIGINT DEFAULT 0,
    joined_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, user_id)
);

CREATE TABLE secret_chats (
    secret_chat_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id_a      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    user_id_b      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    device_id_a    BIGINT NOT NULL,     -- secret chats are per-device
    device_id_b    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    key_fingerprint BIGINT NOT NULL,    -- DH key fingerprint
    ttl_seconds    INT DEFAULT 0,       -- self-destruct
    state          SMALLINT,            -- 1=requested, 2=accepted, 3=active
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE secret_messages (
    secret_chat_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    msg_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
    encrypted_blob BYTEA NOT NULL,      -- server can't decrypt
    sender_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    date           TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (secret_chat_id, msg_id)
);

CREATE TABLE media (
    media_id  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id  BIGINT,
    s3_key    TEXT NOT NULL,
    mime_type TEXT,
    size_bytes BIGINT,
    thumb_s3  TEXT,
    duration  INT,                       -- for video/audio
    width     INT, height INT,
    dc_id     SMALLINT,                  -- which DC has the file
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Redis keys (Session Manager):
--   session:{user_id}:{device_id}  -> {auth_key_id, server_id, last_seq, last_pts}
--   update_queue:{user_id}:{device_id} -> LIST of pending updates (TTL 7d)
--   online:{user_id}                -> SET of device_ids with active connection
--   channel_subscriber_count:{channel_id} -> counter (cached)
--   user_channels:{user_id}         -> SET of channel_ids (for "new post" push)
```

### Indexes
- `messages (user_id, peer_id, msg_id DESC)` — primary key covers, used for history pagination.
- `messages (user_id, date DESC)` — "recent conversations" view.
- `dialogs (user_id, pinned, date DESC)` — chat list with pinned-on-top.
- `chat_members (user_id, chat_id)` — "my groups" list.
- `channel_messages (channel_id, msg_id DESC)` — channel history (only admins read full).
- `channel_subscriptions (user_id, channel_id)` — "my channels" list.
- `secret_messages (secret_chat_id, msg_id DESC)` — secret chat history.

### Storage Choice
- **Per-user message storage** (KV or Postgres-sharded by `user_id`): each user has their own copy of every conversation. Pros: per-user delete is trivial (delete all rows where `user_id=X`); per-user search is local; per-user read state is local. Cons: storage is 2× (one copy per participant). At Telegram scale, this trade-off is acceptable given storage is cheap.
- **Channel messages stored centrally** (not per-subscriber copy) — subscribers fetch via `channels.getMessages`. For large channels, this avoids O(subscribers) writes per post.
- **Redis Cluster** for Session Manager and update queues. 100 TB across 200 shards; 5M ops/s.
- **S3-compatible object storage** (Telegram uses a custom cluster; we use S3) for media; CDN-fronted.
- **Kafka** for cross-DC replication; one topic per DC pair; partitioned by `user_id` for ordering.
- **ScyllaDB** is an alternative to Postgres for messages — write-optimized, linear scalability.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Auth (one-time per device)
- Updates (long-poll / push)
- Hybrid channel fan-out: small channels (<=10k subs) write a copy to each
- Subscriber's inbox (fan-out-on-write). Large channels store centrally and
- Notify subscribers to fetch (fan-out-on-read with push trigger).
- 1. Always write to the channel's central message store
- 2a. Small channel: fan out on write — write a copy to each
- Subscriber's dialogs table and enqueue an updateNewMessage

**Defines:** `ChannelFanoutService`, `SecretChatService`

### API Design (MTProto methods)

```
# Auth (one-time per device)
auth.sendCode              { phone }              -> { phone_code_hash }
auth.signIn                { phone, code, hash }  -> { auth_key, user }

# Cloud chats
messages.sendMessage       { peer, text, random_id, reply_to }  -> { msg_id, date }
messages.getHistory        { peer, offset_id, limit }           -> [messages]
messages.editMessage       { peer, msg_id, new_text }
messages.deleteMessages    { peer, msg_ids[], revoke }
messages.readHistory       { peer, max_id }
messages.search            { peer, query, limit }

# Groups
messages.createChat        { user_ids[], title }
messages.addChatUser       { chat_id, user_id }
messages.forwardMessage    { from_peer, msg_id, to_peer }

# Channels
channels.createChannel     { title, type }
channels.subscribe         { channel_id }
channels.unsubscribe       { channel_id }
channels.getMessages       { channel_id, offset_id, limit }
channels.sendMessage       { channel_id, text }   (admin only)

# Secret chats (E2EE)
messages.requestSecretChat { user_id }            -> { secret_chat_id }
messages.acceptSecretChat  { secret_chat_id, g_a } -> { g_b, key_fingerprint }
messages.sendEncrypted     { secret_chat_id, random_id, encrypted_blob }
messages.getEncryptedHistory { secret_chat_id, offset }

# Media
upload.getFile            { file_id, offset, limit }     (chunked download)
upload.saveFilePart       { file_id, part, bytes }       (chunked upload)
messages.sendMedia        { peer, media_id, caption }

# Updates (long-poll / push)
updates.getState          -> { seq, pts, qts, date }
updates.getDifference     { pts, date, qts }  -> { new_messages, updates }
updates.getChannelDifference { channel_id, pts } -> { messages }

# Bots
bot.start                 { bot_token }
sendMessage (bot API)     { chat_id, text, reply_markup }
setWebhook (bot API)      { url }
```

### Key Algorithms

```python
# Hybrid channel fan-out: small channels (<=10k subs) write a copy to each
# subscriber's inbox (fan-out-on-write). Large channels store centrally and
# notify subscribers to fetch (fan-out-on-read with push trigger).
import asyncio
from typing import List

WRITE_FANOUT_THRESHOLD = 10_000   # above this, switch to read-fanout

class ChannelFanoutService:
    def __init__(self, msg_store, sub_store, session_mgr, push_svc):
        self.msg = msg_store
        self.sub = sub_store
        self.sess = session_mgr
        self.push = push_svc

    async def post_message(self, channel_id, sender_id, text, media_id=None):
        # 1. Always write to the channel's central message store
        msg_id = await self.msg.next_channel_msg_id(channel_id)
        await self.msg.insert_channel_message(
            channel_id, msg_id, sender_id, text, media_id)
        sub_count = await self.sub.subscriber_count(channel_id)

        if sub_count <= WRITE_FANOUT_THRESHOLD:
            # 2a. Small channel: fan out on write — write a copy to each
            # subscriber's dialogs table and enqueue an updateNewMessage
            # push for online subscribers.
            await self._fanout_write(channel_id, msg_id, sender_id, text)
        else:
            # 2b. Large channel: fan out on read — just enqueue a lightweight
            # "new post in channel C" push to subscribers; clients fetch on demand.
            await self._fanout_notify(channel_id, msg_id)

    async def _fanout_write(self, channel_id, msg_id, sender_id, text):
        # Batch-paginate subscribers (1000 at a time) to avoid huge memory
        subs = await self.sub.iter_subscribers(channel_id, batch=1000)
        for batch in subs:
            # Bulk insert into each subscriber's messages table (1 SQL per batch)
            await self.msg.bulk_insert_dialog_entries(
                batch, channel_id, msg_id, sender_id, text)
            # Push updateNewMessage to online subscribers
            online = await self.sess.filter_online(batch)
            await asyncio.gather(*[
                self.sess.enqueue_update(uid, {
                    "type": "updateNewChannelMessage",
                    "channel_id": channel_id, "msg_id": msg_id,
                    "sender_id": sender_id, "text": text})
                for uid in online
            ])

    async def _fanout_notify(self, channel_id, msg_id):
        # For huge channels: just push "channel C has new post" — clients
        # then call channels.getMessages to fetch the actual content.
        # This caps server work at O(online_subscribers) lightweight pings
        # instead of O(all_subscribers) writes.
        subs = await self.sub.iter_subscribers(channel_id, batch=10_000)
        for batch in subs:
            online = await self.sess.filter_online(batch)
            await asyncio.gather(*[
                self.sess.enqueue_update(uid, {
                    "type": "updateChannelTooLong",
                    "channel_id": channel_id,
                    "top_msg_id": msg_id})
                for uid in online
            ])
            # For offline subscribers: NO push (would be 1M+ pushes per post).
            # They see the new post when they next open the channel.
```

```python
# Secret chat E2EE key exchange (Diffie-Hellman over prime p, generator g).
# Server facilitates exchange but cannot derive the shared key.
import secrets, hashlib

class SecretChatService:
    # p, g are well-known Telegram DH params (2048-bit prime)
    P = ...  # 2048-bit safe prime
    G = 7

    async def request(self, initiator_id, initiator_device, recipient_id):
        # Initiator generates a (their secret), publishes g_a = g^a mod p
        a = secrets.randbelow(self.P - 2) + 1
        g_a = pow(self.G, a, self.P)
        sc_id = snowflake()
        await self.db.insert_secret_chat(
            sc_id, initiator_id, recipient_id, initiator_device,
            state="requested", initiator_g_a=g_a)
        # Notify recipient (encrypted on the wire via MTProto, but server-side plaintext)
        await self.session.enqueue_update(recipient_id, {
            "type": "updateNewEncryptedMessage",
            "secret_chat_id": sc_id, "g_a": str(g_a), "state": "requested"})
        return sc_id

    async def accept(self, sc_id, recipient_device, g_a_from_initiator):
        # Recipient verifies g_a is in the valid range (1 < g_a < p-1, and
        # safety checks to prevent small-subgroup attacks), then generates b,
        # publishes g_b = g^b mod p, computes key = g_a^b mod p.
        if not (1 < g_a_from_initiator < self.P - 1):
            raise InvalidKeyError("g_a out of range")
        b = secrets.randbelow(self.P - 2) + 1
        g_b = pow(self.G, b, self.P)
        key = pow(g_a_from_initiator, b, self.P)   # shared secret, server NEVER sees
        key_fingerprint = int.from_bytes(
            hashlib.sha1(str(key).encode()).digest()[-8:], 'big')
        await self.db.update_secret_chat(
            sc_id, state="active", recipient_device=recipient_device,
            key_fingerprint=key_fingerprint)
        # Send g_b back to initiator — they compute key = g_b^a mod p (same value)
        initiator_id = await self.db.get_initiator(sc_id)
        await self.session.enqueue_update(initiator_id, {
            "type": "updateNewEncryptedMessage",
            "secret_chat_id": sc_id, "g_b": str(g_b),
            "key_fingerprint": key_fingerprint, "state": "active"})

    async def store_encrypted(self, sc_id, msg_id, encrypted_blob, sender_id):
        # Server stores the encrypted blob as-is; cannot decrypt.
        await self.db.insert_secret_message(sc_id, msg_id, encrypted_blob, sender_id)
        # Deliver to recipient's device (which has the key to decrypt)
        recipient = await self.db.get_recipient(sc_id)
        await self.session.enqueue_update(recipient, {
            "type": "updateNewEncryptedMessage",
            "secret_chat_id": sc_id, "msg_id": msg_id,
            "encrypted_blob": encrypted_blob, "sender_id": sender_id})

    # Self-destruct: a background sweeper deletes messages older than TTL
    async def sweep_expired(self):
        cutoff = now() - timedelta(seconds=...)
        for sc in await self.db.get_chats_with_ttl():
            await self.db.delete_secret_messages_before(sc.id, cutoff)
```

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **60M concurrent connections**: 2000 proxy servers, 30k connections each. Go's goroutine-per-connection model handles this well; ~30k goroutines per server, ~150 MB RAM. Connection migration: if a proxy dies, client auto-reconnects to another; pending updates are re-fetched via `updates.getDifference` from the Session Manager (which is the source of truth).
- **Update ordering**: each user has a `seq` (sequence number for service updates) and `pts` (position timestamp for messages). Clients report their last `seq` and `pts`; the server sends only newer updates. If a gap is detected, the client calls `updates.getDifference` to backfill. This makes updates idempotent and order-tolerant.
- **Cross-DC consistency**: each user has a "home DC"; writes to that user go through their home DC. Cross-DC replication is async via Kafka (within 1 s). A user connecting to a non-home DC is redirected or proxied. Reads can be served from any DC (eventually consistent).
- **Channel broadcast to 1M subscribers**: hybrid fan-out. Small channels (< 10k) write per-subscriber copies (2× storage trade-off for fast reads). Large channels store centrally and notify subscribers to fetch — saves O(N) writes per post at the cost of O(N) reads when subscribers open the channel (which they do anyway in their normal app usage).
- **Media at 500 TB/day**: chunked upload (256 KB chunks); resumable; chunks stored across multiple S3 nodes; video transcoded async via FFmpeg pipeline; thumbnails generated server-side; CDN edge-cached.
- **MTProto request combining**: clients batch multiple RPC calls into a single TCP message; server batches responses. Reduces RTT overhead — important for mobile networks with 200+ ms RTT.

### Caching Strategy
- **Session state**: always Redis (the source of truth for routing and update queues); write-through.
- **Recent messages**: per-(user, peer) Redis LRU cache of last 100 messages — most reads are recent history.
- **Dialog list**: per-user Redis cache, invalidated on new message.
- **Channel subscriber count**: cached in Redis, refreshed on subscribe/unsubscribe.
- **User profile / channel info**: Redis 1 h TTL; invalidated on update.
- **Media thumbnails**: CDN-edge cached, 7-day TTL.
- **Bot webhook URLs**: Redis, invalidated on bot reconfiguration.

### Failure Modes
- **Proxy crash**: clients reconnect to another proxy; re-fetch pending updates via `updates.getDifference` from Session Manager (Redis is HA, no data loss). In-flight RPCs time out and client retries (idempotent via `random_id`).
- **Session Manager (Redis) unavailable**: fall back to per-proxy local cache; new sessions can't be created (auth fails) but existing connections continue; recovery via Redis Cluster failover (RF=3, automatic).
- **Message Storage shard down**: that shard's users' new messages fail (client retry); reads from replicas. Shard recovery via PITR (point-in-time recovery from WAL).
- **Cross-DC link degraded**: writes queue in Kafka; replication lag grows but eventually catches up. Users connecting to a non-home DC may see stale data temporarily.
- **Push service overwhelmed**: rate-limit pushes (max 1 per user per 30 s); batch messages in a single push ("3 new messages from Alice"); fall back to in-house push if FCM/APNs rate-limited.
- **Media storage (S3) degraded**: uploads fail with retry; downloads fall back to direct origin (slower); CDN serves stale thumbnails.
- **MTProto protocol upgrade**: roll out proxy-by-proxy with old + new protocols coexisting; clients auto-upgrade.
